Messages.Author: Stefan Ferenci
Messages.Body:
Hi all,
just my toughts about the ec in barcelona.

first of all big tourney vtes became a game of luck. 3 rounds is simply not
enough! next years ec should have 5 or 6 rounds using the swiss format!!!
the original archon sucks! since it splits big tourney into groups of 25
players the ec was basically an event which consisted of 3 separate tourneys
and one final. so while some will say they saw heavy stealth bleed in their
part of the tourney i saw a lot of combat and only 1 stealth bleeder!!!!
another sideeffect of the tourney was that people that registered together
also played together (sten and beatrice during, rob treasure and dave
hammond, i and martin, chris and sascha, etc).

anyways on to the tourney:

i wanted to play a stani purge deck, but martin weinmayer convinced me that
i might not have a chance with it and i thought that all my games would be
quite short either winning or losing quite fast, so i decided to switch
decks while waiting to register. since i expected little combat i decided to
play my weenie auspex deck i just played once before ( i played several
versions of wennie, intercept and weenie intercept decks, but this deck i
just put togehter when anarchs were released because i really like martin
(weinmayer) frankel, feo ramos and maldavis. during the tourney i realised
that there were some minor design flaws in this deck, but anyways.
round one: ( i don´t remember names so please don´t be offended) french guy
that talks way to much (arika mind rape)> fun belgium guy (cell with
guns)>cool french guy (cel with guns)>me> martin weinmayer (his famous 66
card tremere intercept wall pool machine deck).
i have a nice draw some blood support (hg with blood doll), some bounce and

martin trys to kill the french guy he taps him self out and i manage to oust
him (after an hour and 30 minutes) i can also oust the frech guy and then we
all agree to withdraw. my pred didn´t have any rushes and was just relying
on bleeds that i was able to soak or bounce so i managed to stay out of
combat with him. 1 gw 3 vps

second round and i am happy, i have the chance to play a game of vampire
with rob treasure.
dave hammond (fatima multirush)>jan? from norway (big malk bleed)> chris
(weenie pot rush)> rob (lasombra vote ?)>me once again playing against two
combat decks.
once again sorry rob. first turn milli smith V.H. rob brought out gratiano
first and got hit with an haven uncovered right away by chrisand brought
down to to blood(gratiano) so he decided to switch places with dave. i then
hit gratiano with a society of leopold and attacked him twice bringin him
down to zero blood thus burining him during his untap phase. when he then
attempted an action with ingnacio i blocked him with my ivory bow guy and
send him to torpor. he then brought out guido lucciano. in my next master
phase i hit guido with a pentex subversion bleed for one and the diablerized
ingnacio. so robs game was pretty much over right after it started. with
rob down on 4 pool his prey having the millicent tried to equip esau with 10
blood with an leather jacket. needless to say i used my eagle sight and some
spare intercept to burn esau. right after i ousted rob, dave came out of his
hand jam and started to attack me i lost a lot of minions, was down on 5
pool ( i didnßt draw a blood doll the whole game). with fatima bothering
chris pot weenies and my aus weenies we agreed that i would play my pentex
sub on fatiama if he would be happy with his one vp. he agreed. i then went
on to oust jan his last action was the removal of the penteyx subversion.
and fatiama started killing my minions again, but eventually dave ran out of
cards was ousted by chris and i ousted chris then.

so one hell of a game 2gw 7 vps.

3 round: 3 potence decks :-((((((((
sascha (wote deck)> me > some spanish guy that should learn english (nossie
princes rush)> smiling tom (reactive euro brujah)> shane spencer (wennie pot
rush)(by the way the aussies were really cool it was fun playing and talking
with them)

while sascha and smiling tom were killed i managed to saty alive and we
withdrew due to time reasons.

so 2 gw 8 vps tie for 3rd with jay (he wins the tiebreaker). seeing combat
all day i had a really bad feeling going to the finals. i thought i really
played a crappy deck and thought i would stand no chance during the finals.
i knew that jay was playing mono auspex (so i expected him playing his nac
deck) and that jo was playing stealth bleed. so assuming that the tatus told
jay what i was playing my game plan was to sit right behind toni and hoping
that jay would try to sit in front of toni (far away from me)so we both
would sandwich him with auspex and i would gain an easy vp. then hold on for
maybe a second or third place finish.
i am not going to bore you with my views on the finals. just a few comments.

after figuring out what everybody played i was sure that jay would win (he
would have would he have drawn a gun and been more aggressive against zsolt)
if jo would have had enough stealth to remove the pentex he would have been
trying to bleed me more often.
if zsolt would have tried to remove the pentex he would have wasted actions
and might not have finished second ( he ousted jo with his last minion) and

jay was afraid of arika and didn´t offer any good deals to toni.
so humble spectators who should ahve removed the pentex?
aranthebenes could and would have been blocked!!!!!!!! i had an eagle sight
in my staring hand and had one in my hand most of the time.
the guns would hurt ne a lot i guess zsolt would have won then (but i had a
society and was hoping for my second pentex)
i really liked zsolts deck but he was almost out of cards when he ousted jo
so he would not have been able to oust me i guess
sorry jo that i didn´t give you enough pool.

finally thanks to damnas and the organizing crew and all the fun players i
meet and had the chance to play with.
robin, dave and jeff i was fun seeing you again and i hope i´ll have the

But that pool of 24 was drawn from the pool of 80. Just because there
were two steps in the random process doesn't mean you were any less
randomly seated.

Prior to the rolling of dice for player number, you would have had a
probability of playing all 12 of those people.
Whether it was broken down into blocks of 24 before actually working
out who you sat with, or just worked randomly fromt he very start
makes no difference.

Imagine a simplified example:
you could play 1 round against one person from a pool of 4. A, B, C,
D.

You're randomly paired, and you get A. there were 4 people with equal
probabilities. therefore it was a 1/4 chance.

Now imagine they were broken into 2 groups first, then you were
assigned a random group, then a random opponent within that group.
possible pairs in groups would be:
AB CD
AC BD
AD BC

each row has a 1/3 chance of happeneing. being assigned to each group
has a 1/2 chance of happeneing.
your chance of playing against A under this scheme is:
1/3 * 1/2 * 1/2
+ 1/3 * 1/2 * 1/2
+ 1/3 * 1/2 * 1/2
= 1/4

same as if you were just randomly sat next to a player at the start,
without breaking it down.

You had 0 chance of playing against the _other_ 12 people from your
pool of 24 once the group of 24 was determined. and you had 0 chance
of playing against the other 56 people in the field once the group was
determined. so whether the people were in your group or not didn't
matter if you weren't playing against them anyway.

salem

This is an interesting thread for me in my function as next years EC head
judge and tournament organizer.

I appreciate all comments about seating and randomness of seating, judging
style and every other aspect related to the organization of the tournament
(not the event!).

Everybody, shoot now.

I like the idea of total randomness of each rounds seating, though. With a
big player field there shouldn´t be too much double team ups because of

While it doesn't make a difference in who *you* play as an individual,
it does make a difference when you consider a group of players. For
example, if I and my 3 buddies all drive together to an 80-person
tournament, it'd be nice to have all 4 of us *not* be in the same
24-person sub-group, for instance, to increase the chances that we
won't all be playing the same opponent - because the odds are good
that we'll talk to each other between rounds about what decks we saw.

Why does this matter at all? I don't think it matters that much - it
certainly doesn't matter statistically, but if you happen to have
figured out partway through round 2 that you're in a 24-person
sub-group, you should be able to identify which tables contain your
sub-group, and that gives you an edge in checking out potential decks
to face - it's much easier to glance at the other 4 tables full of
potential round-3 opponents than it is to glance at the other 14. And
if you have a friend, or 2, or 3 also in that sub-group, that scouting
gets even easier. Yeah, it's the same for everybody else, which helps
bring it back to 'doesn't matter that much.'

I think there's probably some tiny advantage to be gained from the
meta-game deck building process here too; I would hazard to guess that
in most large tournaments, players conciously build decks with a
consideration to 'I know the buddy I am going there with is playing
this deck type, so I won't, so to avoid contesting.' The smaller the
potential pool of decks, the more this benefits the buddies, as it
increases the odds that they would have faced each other eventually,
which is an edge to them that a single foe might not have. (Again, as
salem notes this last point isn't a massive problem because the
determination of which sub-group of players you end up in is totally
random.)

I don't think it's a very significant problem to have a tourney
organizer break groups into sub-groups that play internally; but I do
think there might be some corner-case tiny advantage, especially if
you can determine that this is the case, compared to shuffling the
entire player pool around.

(Now just be thankful that Archon doesn't do things in a Swiss system
where subsequent rounds are grouped by previous GW/VPs!)

-John Flournoy

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
"LSJ" <vte...@white-wolf.com> wrote in message
news:3F97EE8E...@white-wolf.com...
> Stefan Ferenci wrote:

> > yes but i played 12 pplayers out of a pool of 24 players not the 80 that
> > played. that sucks. the vienniese archon just makes random seating every
> > round. more fun
>
> Incorrect.
> 12 out of 24 chosen at random from a set of 80 is no different than 12
> out of 80.

This is true. But what *is* a little different about having
"one big tournament" as opposed to "three parallel 25-player
tournaments" is that in a 25-player tournament, the 12 people
you play against can have played against 12 people that you
didn't play against. In a 75-player tournament, they could
have played against 62 people that you didn't play against.

This doesn't directly affect your preliminary-round
experience, of course. If "strength of opponent's record"
were actually used as a tiebreaker (not currently done for
reasons of being computationally difficult, I believe), it
could matter, I imagine. And it does affect what the people
you played with would be able to tell you about the decks
of the players in the finals (if a finalist came from a
different "pod", no one you played with would have played
against her).

These are very possibly not compelling enough reasons to
go to the effort of making "cross-group randomized" Archon
seating charts for large tournaments. But it's not
*exactly* the same to group players into subsets of 25 as
it is to group them all together in one big set.

Josh

doesn't have this particular problem with eight-player
tournaments

Messages.Author: John Flournoy
Messages.Body:
"Johannes Walch" <johanne...@vekn.de> wrote in message news:<bn919f$5lr$05$1...@news.t-online.com>...


With 171 players there shouldn't need to be ANY double ups, in my
opinion. There's no reason for any player to see the same opponent
twice when you're facing 13 or 14 opponents out of 170 (or some
similarly large number.)

And in terms of 'sheer probability' - I'm not willing to do out the
math, but I'd bet the odds are actually pretty high that a pure
randomization each round will have double-ups, much like the classic
birthday-share probability question that surprises people (How many
random people do you need before getting a 50% chance that any two
share a birthday? Only 23.)

-John Flournoy

>"same" pool you could conceivably see the exact same seating arrangements
>as you do with seperate "pools". The use of the pools saves a hell of a lot of
>coding to enable the archon to handle that many people.

Exactly. If you did do the seating totally randomly each round, but
'tweaked' so that each person never plays at the same table as someone
they've already played against, at the end of the day, i am pretty
sure you would be able to go back and, with enough mind-numbing
analysis, be able to 'create' sub-groups of people who never got to
play against other sub-groups. But those groups would probably all be
of different sizes, potentially being advantageous to those in groups
of certain sizes (i don't care to try and consider if it would be an
advantage to be in a big or a small group, but i would be willing to
assert that if everyone was in as similar sized group as possible,
it'd be more fair). So you're still in groups, you just didn't know
what those groups were prior to each round's seating being generated.

If you decided to generate all seating for all rounds from the total
pool before any round started, you could work out what groups the
people were in before hand, and you'd be injust the same situation as
if you'd uniformly broken the people into groups, except now the
groups are of a random size instead of all equal.

As someone else pointed out, the only disadvantage to prior group
creation is people might be able to get a 'feel' for what group they
are in and scout the approriate tables. But if everyone gets to do
this, what does it matter?
Imagine if seating were pure random. then imagine eah person scouts
one other random table. some of those people will get lucky and scout
decks they are about to face. some people will scout decks they'll
never face. So the people who got lucky get an advantage. Another
random element added in to the mix of trying to work out who's the
best player. Personally, i like to keep the random element as minimal
as possible.

>I'm sure that if you develop the seating charts for a 300 hundered person
>tournament that the powers that be would consider incorperating them.
>But be assured its a pointless exercise.

Maybe not pointless, but definately tedious and not really necessary.



Messages.Author: Flux
Messages.Body:

No, the minimum number of players such that each player never plays anyone
who has played one of his previous opponents is 125 (assuming 3 rounds and
5-players per table). However, the set of players that your opponents have
played against can be greater than 24, 24 is actually the minimal solution
(assuming no repeated pairs).

>> These are very possibly not compelling enough reasons to
>> go to the effort of making "cross-group randomized" Archon
>> seating charts for large tournaments. But it's not
>> *exactly* the same to group players into subsets of 25 as
>> it is to group them all together in one big set.
>
>
> Those who desire more cross-group randomization are free to
> start with the optimal seating chart and then randomly swap
> a player or two between each "pod".

For two rounds, 25 players is the optimal solution. So, any swapping needs
only be made in the third round, which simplifies the problem considerably.
Then the number of players that is _not_ swapped should be inversely
proportional to the number of 25 player sets (ie, 1/2 for 50 players, 1/3
for 75, etc...).

This was going to be a simple example, but I ended up writing a full
solution for 25-player sets: ;)

Let A, B, C... denote the sets of 25 players. Take the seatings for the
third round as made in optimal seating chart as
A1-A2-A3-A4-A5 A6-A7-... ...
B1-B2-B3-B4-B5 B6-B7-... ...
...

If you're at a 50-player tournament, you should swap half those player. So,
the seating becomes
A1-B2-A3-B4-A5 A6-B7-...
B1-A2-B3-A4-B5 B6-A7-...

If you're at a 75-player tournament, you should swap 2/3 of the players. The
seating becomes
A1-B2-C3-A4-B5 ...
B1-C2-A3-B4-C5 ...
C1-A2-B3-C4-A5 ...

At a 100-player tournament it's
A1-B2-C3-D4-A5 ...
B1-C2-D3-A4-B5 ...
C1-D2-A3-B4-C5 ...
D1-A2-B3-C4-D5 ...

...and so for a 125 player tournament, it would be
A1-B2-C3-D4-E5 ...
B1-C2-D3-E4-A5 ...
C1-D2-E3-A4-B5 ...
D1-E2-A3-B4-C5 ...
E1-A2-B3-C4-D5 ...

There are a number of permutations that can be made from these for
randomization. There is also the matter of how to deal with a number of
players that is not a multiple of 25 (including 4-player tables). I leave
those issues as an exercise to the reader. :)

Of course, since you're dealing with fractions of 5-player tables you can
never have an exact, perfectly balanced solution without using a chainsaw.
Feel free to use one if someone complains about this small imbalance. ;)

Flux

respective games went, or how respective opponents play, could fall
under the category of 'outside assistance' which is illegal, yeah...

discussing each other's decks between rounds - not just friends, but
with whomever happened to be handy. Admittedly, I haven't been to a
regional/national tournament in a couple of years, but still.

Is there some provision in the rules that I didn't see that says
'scouting other decks once you're ousted is illegal'? Is it
technically illegal to discuss how completed games or rounds or decks
of a tournament have turned out between rounds (or so long as all the
players are not actively in the middle of a game?)

I routinely inform judges if I see something that is not legal

Messages.Author: Johannes Walch
Messages.Body:
> Computer-random is different from Archon-random which I was referring
> to. I always wondered about computer random though.. can't you just
> include an input from the clock (the microsecond it gets checked or
> whatever) to make it genuinely random?

No. Because even with the input of a clock it is just randomly seeded
predetermined patterns. The only way of "real" random data in computers are
extension cards (e.g PCI) which feature an old-style analogue tube which
generates noise. This noise is processed by some A/D converter and more
stuff and the result is the best "random" you can get in computers.

But as you can imagine this type of hardware is rather expensive, difficult
to handle AND most of all unecessary for joe average (like me).

There are limitations to how much 'randomization' you can do though.
Consider that for each number of players, there is a finite number of
permutations. You have to pick three, but most groupings will be ruled out
by the seating rules and guidelines. Most of the ones that are left are
actually equal with a simple permutation of the initial seating.

This means that in some cases you have no choice, the guidelines force you
to a certain pattern of seatings, which is the optimal seating pattern
presented by the Archon.

However, as the number of players increases, so should the number of valid
seatings.

I think reading the system time (once) is random enough. However, there are
problems with doing it repeatedly... (see below)

> If a computer can randomise the seed -why shouldn't it randomise the
> pattern?

Because the program always runs the same way. Imagine getting the random
seed from the system clock every time. Since the program always runs the
same way, it will always take the same time to pick up the second 'random'
seed. So, if the first seed is the same, so will the second, and you're no
better off than simply calculating a pattern from the first seed. And,
you're quite likely to get the same reading from the system time anyway,
unless your program runs really slow. :)

Just did a quick test with a simple 'roll dice' program: when seeding every
roll from the system time I can get over 100.000 consecutive rolls with the
same result. When using a rand() routine, I got different results every time
I tested it. Obviously a 'pseudo-random' pattern is preferable. :)

Flux
